name: Lower trap / serratus work
lead: Lower trapezius and serratus anterior work refers to exercises aimed at the muscles that control the shoulder blade (scapula). The lower trapezius pulls the scapula down and helps rotate it upward, while the serratus anterior pulls it forward around the rib cage; together with the upper trapezius they sustain upward rotation for overhead arm movement.[1][2]

People train these muscles to look better by improving upper-body posture: stronger scapular stabilisers are said to pull the shoulders down and back, counter rounded shoulders and a hunched upper back, and give a broader, more upright look. Lower and mid-trap development also adds visible thickness to the upper back.[4][5]

Wikipedia's article on upper crossed syndrome, the combination of forward head posture and rounded shoulders, describes the middle and lower trapezius as stretched and weak in that pattern, and lists strengthening of the mid and lower back and scapular retractors among suggested approaches, while noting that support for the recommendations is thin.[3] Lifters on T Nation describe the lower traps as often under-trained relative to the upper traps.[6][7]

chain: Shoulder blades sit lower and flatter against the ribcage
angle.text: The aim is to change how the shoulders and upper back sit, so the frame looks more open and upright. Practitioners add rows, wide-grip pulling and similar exercises to routines for rounded shoulders.

infobox: Shoulder posture, scapular stability, upper-back look

paras: The trapezius has upper, middle and lower fibres. The lower fibres arise from the lower thoracic vertebrae and depress and upwardly rotate the scapula, working with the serratus anterior and opposing the levator scapulae and rhomboids.[1]

The serratus anterior arises from the outer surfaces of the upper nine ribs and attaches along the inner border of the scapula, supplied by the long thoracic nerve. It protracts the scapula, nicknamed the boxer's muscle for its role in punching, and its lower part rotates the scapula so the arm can be raised.[2]

Damage to the long thoracic nerve is the most common cause of winged scapula, and the nerve is vulnerable in some surgeries such as axillary lymph node clearance.[2] Trapezius dysfunction can cause winged scapula and abnormal scapular movement, and accessory nerve palsy can cause shoulder drooping and pain.[1]

sections.h: Use in posture and lifting communities
paras: Exercises for these muscles appear in posture routines for rounded shoulders and forward-head posture.[3] On T Nation, one user says pulldown variations hit the mid back, rhomboids and lower traps, which he describes as the muscles that bring the scapula into posterior tilt.[4]

Several lifters report a physical therapist telling them that heavy overhead and pressing work had left the upper traps stronger than the middle and lower traps; they describe a fix built around wide-grip pulling work and less overhead pressing.[6][7] Another log describes loaded carries as a way to strengthen the "scapular stabilizers", naming the lower traps.[5]

No studies found on lower trap or serratus strengthening specifically as a posture or appearance intervention. The upper crossed syndrome article cites one randomized trial on thoracic manipulation and neck pain, which is a different intervention.[3]

lore.intro: On T Nation, lower traps are described as commonly weak relative to upper traps, and lifters share rehab-style pulling work that targets them.[5][6][7]

claims.claim: Weak lower traps and strong upper traps cause shoulders to look elevated or rounded.
claims.believers: Lifters report being told by physical therapists that excess overhead work left upper traps dominant, and one poster describes elevated shoulder blades on a hunched lifter.[4][6][7]
claims.experts: Wikipedia describes weak, stretched middle and lower trapezius in upper crossed syndrome and notes that its treatment support is thin.[3]

claims.claim: Wide-grip pulling and rows strengthen the lower traps and improve posture.
claims.believers: Posters recommend high-rep, wide-grip cable and pulldown work to rebalance the shoulders.[4][7]
claims.experts: No trials were found testing these exercises for posture or looks.

card.summary: Exercises for the shoulder-blade muscles used in posture routines; anatomy is well described, appearance benefit untested.
card.note: Sources cover anatomy and nerve injury, not training outcomes.

quick.overview:
The lower trapezius and serratus anterior steer the shoulder blade. Posture communities train them to counter rounded shoulders.

Anatomy sources describe their roles; no study found tests this training for posture or looks.
quick.mechanism: The lower trapezius depresses and rotates the scapula and the serratus anterior pulls it around the ribcage, together stabilising it during arm movement.
quick.risks: Low risk in general. Persistent winging or shoulder pain can reflect nerve injury and is a clinical matter.
